content: In May 2015, the Sixty-eighth World Health Assembly acknowledged the significant public health threat posed by antimicrobial resistance by adopting the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance. This plan outlines strategies to combat antimicrobial resistance, including reducing the unnecessary use of antimicrobials in both humans and animals. It also emphasizes the importance of a cross-sectoral One Health approach, which involves collaboration across disciplines such as human and veterinary medicine. Recognizing the urgency of addressing antimicrobial resistance, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) also adopted resolutions in 2015 to support the Global Action Plan. Many antimicrobials used in food-producing animals are identical or closely related to those used in human medicine. Similarly, antimicrobials used in plant production, such as in orchards, are often the same or closely related to those used in humans. In food-producing animals, antimicrobials are used not only to treat and control bacterial infections but also for disease prevention and growth promotion, even in the absence of disease. However, this practice can lead to the selection and spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in animals, which can then be transmitted to humans through food and other routes. In 2005, the World Health Organization (WHO) established criteria to classify medically important antimicrobials as important, highly important, or critically important for human medicine. These criteria were used to create the WHO List of Critically Important Antimicrobials for Human Medicine (WHO CIA List), which has been regularly updated, with the fifth revision published in 2017. The WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations and best practices for the use of medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals, aiming to preserve their effectiveness for both human and veterinary medicine. These guidelines align with the WHO Global Action Plan. The guidelines were developed using the WHO guideline development process, which included identifying priority questions, systematically reviewing evidence, and formulating recommendations. The process was overseen by the WHO Steering Group and the Guideline Development Group (GDG), which consisted of external experts. The recommendations were based on evidence from systematic reviews and narrative literature reviews, with the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach used to assess the quality of evidence. The GDG made several strong recommendations despite low-quality evidence, as the potential human health benefits of reducing antimicrobial resistance outweighed any potential harms. For example, the GDG recommended a complete restriction on the use of medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals for growth promotion and disease prevention in the absence of clinical diagnosis. Evidence shows that restricting antimicrobial use in animals reduces the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in bacteria that can be transmitted to humans. Broad restrictions across all antimicrobial classes were found to be more effective than narrow restrictions targeting a single class or drug. The GDG also suggested that critically important antimicrobials for human medicine should not be used for controlling or treating infectious diseases in food-producing animals unless no other options are available, as determined by bacterial culture and sensitivity testing. Exceptions to these recommendations may be made to prevent harm to animal health and welfare, but only under strict veterinary oversight. Best practice statements were also formulated, emphasizing that any new class of antimicrobials developed for human use should be considered critically important unless otherwise categorized by WHO. Additionally, medically important antimicrobials not currently used in food production should not be introduced for such purposes in the future. The guidelines apply universally, regardless of region or income level, but special considerations may be needed for implementation in lowand middle-income countries. These include improving animal health management, disease prevention strategies, and laboratory capacity for bacterial culture and sensitivity testing. International organizations like FAO and OIE may assist with implementation. Countries are encouraged to conduct surveillance and monitoring of antimicrobial use in food-producing animals to evaluate the impact of these guidelines. WHO will continue to monitor research developments related to antimicrobial use in food-producing animals and plans to review and update these guidelines five years after publication, or earlier if significant new evidence emerges.
